A SEA OF TRASH FLOODS THE RIVER BESIDE BACLARAN CHURCH A massive accumulation of garbage from Manila Bay filled the river in front of Baclaran Church in Parañaque City on Monday, August 10, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or Habagat swept debris into the area. The thick layer of floating waste created an alarming scene, with trash covering a large portion of the waterway. Nearby residents said they had never experienced anything like this before, highlighting the unusual scale of the debris buildup following the heavy rainfall. The incident once again raises concerns about waste management, waterways, and the impact of heavy rains on communities near Manila Bay. While Quezon City is drowning, where is Vince? Cars are being swallowed by floodwaters. Major roads have turned into rivers. Residents are struggling to get through streets that should never have become impassable. And yet, one question keeps rising above the floodwater: #NasaanSiVince? Where is DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon while Quezon City is once again experiencing severe flooding? This is not about blaming him for the rain. It is about holding him accountable for the infrastructure his department is responsible for. Inspections are not enough. Press releases are not enough. Promises are not enough. When flood-control projects are supposed to protect communities, the public has every right to ask whether those projects are actually working. Because when the roads become rivers and cars become floating objects, something clearly isn't working. So, Secretary Vince Dizon, where are you? The public doesn't need another photo opportunity beside a flooded road. They need answers. They need action. And most of all, they need to know why—after billions have been poured into flood-control infrastructure—Filipinos are still drowning in the same streets. #NasaanSiVince See less While Quezon City is drowning, where is Vince?

August 29, 2026 — One can scarcely imagine the terror: standing inside your own home, hearing the roar of water, mud, and rocks approaching — and having only seconds to wonder if your family will survive. That was the reality for communities along the Nepal–Tibet border on August 26, 2026, when a massive glacier and rock collapse triggered a catastrophic flash flood along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers. Homes, roads, bridges, power plants, and entire settlements were swept away — often with little or no warning.  IN THOSE FINAL MOMENTS Residents were forced to scramble to rooftops, balconies, or any higher ground available — clinging to hope as waters rose nearly 30 feet in half an hour. We may never fully know what went through their minds: Were they crying? Calling loved ones? Praying? Holding each other? What we do know is that behind every statistic is a human life, a family, and a story of heartbreak.  THE SCALE OF LOSS - 469 confirmed dead — and still rising - Hundreds more remain missing, including tourists and pilgrims from several nations - Entire communities buried under mud and debris - Rescue teams continue to reach isolated areas "Behind every number is a family waiting. Behind every missing person is someone desperately hoping. And behind every survivor is a story of courage."  May rescuers reach those still waiting. May the missing be found. And may every grieving family find strength in this time of unimaginable loss.  ,///Charlie. #PrayForNepal #NepalFlood #HimalayanDisaster #FlashFlood #DisasterAwareness #HopeAndPrayer #BosesNgPilipinas See less LOOK:|BEHIND EVERY NUMBER: THE HUMAN HEARTBREAK OF NEPAL’S FLASH FLOOD.

#1DNews | Davao, Philippines  FLOOD ALERT | Street Flooding Hits Carmelite Area in Bajada Following Hours of Rain LOOK: Residents of the Carmelite area in Bajada, Davao City, experienced street flooding early Wednesday, July 1, after several hours of continuous rainfall overnight. According to residents, flooding in the area is a recurring problem whenever heavy rains persist for more than two hours. As of this morning, floodwaters had reportedly risen from knee to waist level in some sections, affecting road access and threatening nearby homes, vehicles, and other properties. While residents noted that floodwaters typically recede within two to three hours after the rain stops, many continue to express concern over the recurring flooding and the damage it brings to their belongings and daily activities. Authorities are advising motorists and the public to exercise caution when passing through flood-prone areas. When the Waters Rise in Davao City, So Do the Online Critics Following the heavy rains brought by the Habagat and recent weather systems on July 24, 2026, several neighborhoods across Davao City once again faced rising floodwaters. From Mandug and Tugbok down to low-lying areas like Bangkal, Matina, and Talomo, families had to endure another stressful night of monitoring river levels, moving to higher ground, or waiting for emergency teams. And like clockwork, as soon as photos of flooded streets flooded social media, the comments section lit up with the usual outrage, political potshots, and online bashing. "Where did the billions go?" "Why hasn't the city solved flooding yet?" It is completely understandable for affected residents to feel frustrated when water enters their homes. But using these calamities to mock or tear down the city overlooks the actual science, geography, and non-stop work happening on the ground. Here is the perspective every Dabawenyo and onlooker needs to hear. 1. You Cannot Out-Engineer a Catch Basin No politician, regardless of their party, and no amount of infrastructure spending can change basic topography. Davao City sits beside major river systems (Davao, Talomo, Matina, Lipadas, Bunawan, and Lasang) flowing straight into the gulf. Key areas like Bago Gallera, Talomo Proper, Ulas, Bangkal, and Matina are natural catch basins. When continuous rains hit the highlands upstream, millions of gallons of water naturally rush downward into these lower elevations. Add a high tide at the coast, and the ocean acts like a giant dam, preventing river mouths from discharging into the sea. Dikes and pumping stations can help manage overflow, but they cannot stop gravity or push back the ocean. 2. Nature Remembers Its Original Shape Parts of Boulevard, Bucana, Agdao, and Sta. Ana were historically mudflats, swamps, and coastal wetlands. Humans can pave over these landscapes with roads, subdivisions, and concrete structures, but when extreme rainfall happens, water simply reclaims its natural pathways. With climate change intensifying weather patterns nationwide, rainfall volumes that used to happen once every few decades are now occurring multiple times a year. This is a regional and global environmental challenge, not an isolated municipal flaw. 3. "Where Did the Funds Go?" Look at the Defense Systems in Place Critics often point to multi-billion flood control budgets as if money should make water instantly disappear. But flood mitigation infrastructure isn't meant to stop rain from falling; it's built to slow down water, protect riverbanks, and buy critical time.  Pumping Stations & Retarding Basins: Built in notorious bottlenecks (like Sasa and La Verna) to hold runoff and force water past high-tide barriers.  Revetment Walls & Dikes: Miles of concrete dikes line the Matina, Talomo, and Davao rivers to keep riverbanks from completely collapsing during sudden surges.  Early Warning & River Monitoring: The City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO) operates automated sensors and live HD monitoring cameras along all six major river channels, allowing them to issue preemptive siren alarms and evacuation orders hours before water peaks. 4. While Keyboard Warriors Bash, Responders Are Out in the Dark While critics type away in dry rooms, hundreds of frontline responders, from the CDRRMO, BFP, Davao Light, urban search and rescue (SAR) units, and barangay disaster teams, are out in waist-deep water, executing rescue operations, clearing clogged channels, and moving stranded families to safety. Good governance in a coastal, river-dense city isn't measured by the complete absence of natural calamities; it’s measured by preparedness, quick response, and zero casualties. The fact that emergency teams can track upstream river swells in real-time and mobilize rescue trucks within minutes is proof of a functional disaster system. Bashing Davao City during a flood won't lower the tide, and weaponizing human suffering for online arguments won't stop the rain. Instead of tearing each other down, let’s focus on what actually keeps us safe: community preparedness and cooperation. When the CDRRMO issues a Code Red or sounds the warning siren, do not wait. Follow evacuation protocols early. Look out for elderly neighbors, keep your emergency kits ready, and respect the responders risking their safety on the frontlines.

DAVAO: THE “FLOOD CAPITAL” — BUT PERHAPS NOT FOR THE REASON YOU THINK They say Davao is the “Flood Capital of the Philippines.” Well, if someone insists on giving us that crown, perhaps we should wear it proudly—but let’s first ask a simple question: What exactly is overflowing?  Yes, Davao experiences floods. We have rivers that swell after relentless rain, low-lying communities that sometimes bear the brunt of nature, sudden downpours that seem to arrive without an appointment, and roads that occasionally transform into temporary swimming pools. That is a real problem. It deserves real solutions—not political theater. But if we are going to compare cities, perhaps the scoreboard deserves more than a political slogan. During the severe southwest monsoon flooding in July 2025, for example, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority reported hundreds of flooding incidents across Metro Manila within a single day. Rain does not ask who you voted for before it pours. And rivers certainly don't read campaign speeches.  But here's where I see Davao differently. Because there is another kind of flooding happening here—one that doesn't destroy homes, close roads, or leave mud behind. Davao floods with culture. Walk through this city and you encounter a living mosaic of Mindanao: Indigenous traditions, migrant communities, different languages, cuisines, beliefs, stories, and histories woven together into one constantly evolving urban tapestry. Ask someone where they came from, and you may discover an entire story behind the answer. Then, inevitably, there's food. Because in Davao, you can start a conversation about almost anything and somehow end up discussing durian.  “This variety is sweeter.” “No, that one has better texture.” “You haven't tried the best one yet.” Suddenly, what began as a casual conversation has transformed into an international conference on durian. No registration fee required.  But perhaps Davao's most remarkable flood is neither water nor culture. It is warmth. There is a quiet generosity in the character of many Dabawenyos that statistics cannot measure. You can arrive as a stranger and, before long, someone may already be telling you where to eat, what places to visit, which shortcut to take—and, most importantly, which road to avoid when traffic is terrible. That's not just hospitality. That's hospitality with a built-in traffic advisory.  And then there is Davao's natural beauty. The sea. Samal. Mount Apo. The forests. The farms. The rivers. The mountains. The wide spaces that remind you that progress and nature do not always have to be enemies. Davao is also changing. Businesses are arriving. Buildings are rising. Infrastructure is expanding. Communities are growing. People continue to come—not only because they are looking for jobs, but because they are looking for possibilities. Some arrive carrying résumés. Others arrive carrying business plans. Some arrive carrying nothing more than a dream. And somewhere along the way, many discover something unexpected: They don't merely live in Davao. They become part of it. That, perhaps, is the real story. A city should not be judged solely by the problems that rise within it. It should also be judged by what its people continue to build despite those problems. Davao is not perfect. We have traffic. We have growing pains. We have environmental concerns. We have infrastructure challenges. We have political disagreements. And, of course, we have social-media experts who can apparently repair the entire country using nothing but a smartphone and a Facebook account.  But beneath all the noise is something far more difficult to construct: Character. You can build a highway. You can build skyscrapers. You can build malls, bridges, offices, and massive developments. You can even build a spectacular roundabout that everyone will complain about for months.  But you cannot manufacture belonging. You cannot pour it into concrete. You cannot buy it from a catalog. It has to grow. And Davao has grown through people. People from different places came here. They planted roots. They built families. They opened businesses. They raised children. They created communities. And little by little, their individual stories became part of the larger story of the city. And in those years, I have seen something that no flood statistics can capture. I have seen people flood others with smiles, generosity, and warmth.
